screens.title: Where to Cache: Locality and Tiers
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll explore where to place caches in a distributed system, and why proximity to the consumer and the data source matters. You will learn the two core ideas of cache locality — temporal and spatial locality — and then see a practical map of typical cache tiers: browser, CDN, DNS, web server reverse proxy, application caches, and database caches. Each tier offers a different balance of speed, capacity, and consistency. For example, a browser cache gives you zero network latency for hits but limited capacity and control, whereas a distributed Redis cache gives shared state and control at the cost of network hops. We’ll also cover common mistakes, like overly aggressive cache headers or failing to purge CDN content. By the end you should be able to pick the right tier for static assets, A P I responses, and frequently accessed database records, and to explain why a multi-layered cache strategy often provides the best overall performance. Think about a request your app receives — which cache would you want it to hit first, and why?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Where to Cache
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this lesson: locality, tiers, trade-offs

Where to Cache: Locality and Tiers

Understand why cache placement matters and how a layered strategy uses multiple caches to reach both low latency and good capacity.

Orientation
Latency improves when caches are closer to users; capacity and consistency improve farther from the edge. We’ll place caches where their strengths best match the data profile.
Why it matters
Proper tiering reduces origin load, speeds responses, and controls cost. Misplaced caches cause stale content or wasted memory.
Explore Key Topics
Cache Locality
Temporal vs spatial locality and how each guides prefetch and retention strategies.
Cache Tiers
Browser, CDN, DNS, reverse proxy, app cache, and DB caches — purpose and trade-offs for each.
Invalidation & Consistency
TTL, purge, conditional requests, and when revalidation is better than immediate eviction.
Cache Tier Map
A simplified flow shows where a request may be answered before it reaches the origin.
Browser
Zero network latency for hits; limited capacity.
CDN
Edge caching for global reach; requires invalidation strategy.
App / Redis
Shared fast cache for computed or DB-heavy results.
Try to imagine a request for a user profile image: a browser cache may serve it instantly. If not present, the CDN edge may have it. If the CDN misses, the origin web server or S3 will be contacted. This cascading path is the heart of cache tier design.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this module you will be able to explain cache locality, recognize common cache tiers, evaluate trade-offs, and design a layered caching approach. First, you will learn the difference between temporal locality, where recently used data is likely to be used again, and spatial locality, where nearby data is likely to be accessed. Second, you will map caching tiers from browser and CDN down to application and database caches, noting speed and capacity differences. Third, you will weigh trade-offs such as latency, consistency, and cost when choosing where to cache. Finally, you will outline a multi-layer strategy that places caches to catch hot requests early while keeping slower, larger caches for broader coverage. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check when you’ve reached practical readiness. You’ll practice choosing a tier for example assets like images, A P I responses, and database records to reinforce these concepts.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Learning Objectives

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE: Can you pick a tier and list two trade-offs for it?
Mnemonic & Scenarios

Scenario: Profile images
Use CDN for global delivery and browser cache for repeat visits. Purge CDN on updates.
Scenario: API results
Cache at web server or app layer if results are expensive and shareable; avoid browser cache for personalized results without careful headers.

screens.title: Cache Locality: Temporal and Spatial
screens.narratorSegment: Cache locality is the idea that some data is more likely to be accessed again soon, or that data near a recently accessed item will also be accessed. Temporal locality is simply recency: if a user just viewed a product page, they are likely to request related assets soon. Spatial locality is proximity: when you fetch a user record you often need nearby fields or related records like recent activity or addresses. These two principles shape caching behavior: temporal locality suggests keeping recently used items in fast caches; spatial locality suggests prefetching or caching surrounding data structures to reduce future misses. For example, an e-commerce product page load benefits from caching product metadata and adjacent stock levels because a user might open the reviews or similar products. A common misconception is treating all repeated access patterns as temporal locality — some workloads show locality only across related keys, not the identical key. That difference changes whether you design a time-based TTL or a prefetch rule for related keys. Key takeaway: match the cache strategy to observed access patterns — short TTLs for purely temporal hotspots, and grouped caches or prefetch for spatially correlated reads. To test your understanding, ask: does the workload ask for the same exact keys again, or for keys in the same cluster?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Temporal = recency; spatial = nearby data. Both guide retention and prefetch strategies.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Cache Locality

Temporal vs Spatial Locality

Understand both patterns so you cache what will actually be reused.

Temporal locality
Keep recently accessed items for short windows. Use short TTLs and LRU policies to catch hotspots that are repeat-accessed.
Spatial locality
Group related keys or prefetch neighboring data when access patterns show clusters of related fields or records.
Example
Loading a user profile often reads the name, email, and recent activity together. Caching the whole object or prefetching adjacent data avoids multiple round trips.
Common mistake
Assuming temporal locality is universal; some systems have spatial patterns requiring grouped caching instead of simple TTLs.
Visual: Prefetch & Retention
Short TTL + LRU
Catches rapid temporal hotspots while freeing memory quickly when access drops.
Group cache / Prefetch
Load related fields together when spatial locality predicts clustered reads.
Key takeaway
Measure your access patterns. Use temporal retention for repeated single-key hits, spatial grouping for related multi-key reads.

screens.title: Browser Cache (Client-Side)
screens.narratorSegment: The browser cache is the cache closest to the user and can deliver assets with effectively zero network latency when a hit occurs. Browsers store static files — images, C S S, JavaScript, and sometimes entire H T M L responses — guided by HTTP headers like Cache-Control and Expires. This makes repeat visits much faster and reduces server bandwidth. However, capacity is limited by the browser and device, and developers have limited direct control: aggressive caching can cause stale content, while missing headers force unnecessary downloads. A concrete example: if a site serves a logo with Cache-Control: max-age=86400, the browser will reuse that logo for a day unless a conditional request is made. A common mistake is using long TTLs for dynamic content like user dashboards; that causes users to see stale personal data. Use browser caching for static, versioned assets and rely on cache-busting filenames or short TTLs with revalidation for assets that change. When choosing a cache strategy, think of the browser cache as the fastest but least controllable layer in the cache hierarchy. Browser Cache (Client-Side) means closest to user: fastest for hits but limited capacity and developer control; ideal for versioned static assets.. In practical terms, fast local storage for static assets with limited control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Browser Cache

Browser (Client-Side) Cache

Local storage for static assets. Fast, but limited control and capacity.

How it works
Browser stores files and metadata from HTTP headers; conditional requests can revalidate with ETag or Last-Modified.
Example
An image served with Cache-Control: max-age=86400 will be reused by the browser for 24 hours unless revalidated or cache-busted.
Common mistake
Applying long cache TTLs to dynamic personal content and causing stale user views.
Pro tip
Use content-hashed filenames for static assets so browsers can cache indefinitely and updates are safe.
Visual: trade-offs
Speed
Zero network latency for hits.
Capacity & Control
Limited by browser; eviction and TTLs not directly controlled by the server beyond headers.
Use cases
Versioned images, JS/CSS bundles, and static HTML that tolerates revalidation.
Key Takeaway
Use the browser cache for static, versioned assets; avoid long TTLs for personalized content unless revalidation is in place.

screens.title: Content Delivery Network (CDN)
screens.narratorSegment: CDNs are geographically distributed proxy caches that bring static resources closer to users by storing copies on edge servers. When a user requests a file, the CDN routes the request to the nearest edge server and serves cached content if available, reducing latency and origin load. CDNs are ideal for large static assets, videos, and globally popular resources. They also sometimes cache dynamically generated content when configured with care. The trade-offs are clear: CDNs offer large capacity and global coverage, but they add an extra network hop and require an invalidation approach when origin content changes. For example, updating a site logo requires purging the cached object or versioning the filename, otherwise users may continue to see the old image. Security considerations include not caching sensitive personal data unless it is encrypted or properly segmented. A common mistake is trusting default CDN TTLs without aligning them to application semantics. Use CDNs for wide distribution of static assets and for reducing origin bandwidth; for frequently changing per-user data, prefer closer caches with better invalidation control. Content Delivery Network (CDN) means distributed edge cache for global performance; strong for static and broadly-accessed content, requires careful invalidation.. In practical terms, edge caching that brings content geographically closer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › CDN Cache

Content Delivery Network (CDN)

Edge servers store copies of content to reduce latency and origin load for geographically distributed users.

When to use
Large static files, videos, globally accessed assets, and cacheable API responses with controlled invalidation.
Safety note
Avoid caching sensitive personal data at the edge unless it’s encrypted and access is controlled.
Pro tip
Version static asset filenames when possible to avoid complex purge operations.
Common mistake
Relying solely on TTLs without a purge strategy for frequent updates.
Visual: edge benefits
Latency
Reduces geographical latency by serving from nearby edge nodes.
Offload
Decreases origin bandwidth and protects backend from traffic spikes.
Invalidation
Requires purge endpoints or versioning to ensure updated content reaches users quickly.
Key Takeaway
Use CDNs for global static delivery and high-throughput assets; plan invalidation or versioning for updates.

screens.title: DNS Cache
screens.narratorSegment: DNS caching is different from application caches because it caches name-to-IP mappings rather than resource content. DNS resolvers at the operating system, local resolver, and ISP level store records with a TTL so repeated lookups avoid full recursive resolution. This speeds the connection setup phase for users and lowers the cost of name resolution across the network. A TTL determines how long a record is considered valid. DNS caching is not a substitute for content caching, but it plays a crucial role in initial connection latency. A misconception is to treat short DNS TTLs as harmless — changing DNS frequently can lead to higher resolution load and potential propagation delays. Use appropriate TTLs: short for rapidly changing endpoints during migrations, longer for stable services. Remember, DNS impacts how quickly users reach your caches and origin, but it does not cache the payloads themselves. DNS Cache means caches domain-to-ip answers with ttls; reduces lookup latency but is not a content cache.. In practical terms, name resolution caching to speed connection setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › DNS Cache

DNS Caching

Caches name resolution results at several levels to speed connection setup and reduce network lookups.

Where cached
Local OS cache, ISP resolver, public DNS services. Each obeys the record’s TTL.
Example
A DNS record with TTL=300 seconds will be reused for five minutes, avoiding full lookups during that window.
Common mistake
Setting very low TTLs for stable services increases resolver load and may not speed up migrations as expected.
Practical impact
DNS caching reduces the latency of establishing connections to your CDN or origin. It does not replace content caches but complements them by shortening the path to cached resources.
Key takeaway
Tune DNS TTLs according to how frequently endpoints change: short for migrations, longer for stable services to reduce lookup load.

screens.title: Web Server Cache (Reverse Proxy)
screens.narratorSegment: A web server or reverse proxy cache sits at the edge of your server infrastructure and can absorb high volumes of requests before they reach application servers. Tools like Nginx can be configured to cache responses based on URL and headers and to set different TTLs per status code. This approach is effective for non-personalized content such as landing pages or A P I responses that are cacheable. Compared to an app cache, a web server cache is easier to deploy for full responses and can significantly reduce backend load. However, invalidation and personalization are more complex; personalized responses must bypass the cache or use vary headers. The provided Nginx config demonstrates basic caching: define the cache path and key, enable proxy_cache, and set proxy_cache_valid for TTL rules. A common pitfall is caching HTTP responses that include user-specific content without appropriate Vary headers or cache keys. Key takeaway: use reverse proxy caches for broad, non-personalizable responses and be explicit about keys and TTLs. Web Server Cache (Reverse Proxy) means caches application responses at the front door to reduce backend load; best for non-personalized content.. In practical terms, offload traffic at the entry point with nginx-style caching. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Web Server Cache

Reverse proxy caching with Nginx

Place a cache at the entry point to absorb traffic, especially for non-personalized responses.

Example Nginx configuration
proxy_cache_path /var/cache/nginx levels=1:2 keys_zone=my_cache:10m inactive=60m;
proxy_cache_key "$scheme$request_method$host$request_uri";

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://my_upstream_app;
    proxy_cache my_cache;
    proxy_cache_valid 200 302 10m; # Cache successful responses for 10 minutes
    proxy_cache_valid 404 1m;     # Cache 404s for 1 minute
    add_header X-Cache-Status $upstream_cache_status;
  }
}
When to use
Landing pages, public APIs, and static site content that tolerates caching.
Gotcha
Be careful with personalization — missing Vary or incorrect keys cause leakage of user data to others.
Comparison: Web server vs App cache
Web server caches full HTTP responses and are easy to deploy at the edge of your cluster. Application caches store structured data or computed results for reuse across requests and provide finer-grained control.
Speed vs Control
Reverse proxies are simpler for whole-response caching; app caches are better for selective, shared computed values.
Key takeaway
Use web server caching to protect backends from common public requests, and application caches for dynamic, shareable dataset caching.

screens.title: Application Cache: In-process vs Distributed
screens.narratorSegment: Application caching sits where your code runs and often determines the most strategic cache decisions in an architecture. There are two common forms: in-process caches and distributed caches. In-process caches live inside each application instance and offer the absolute lowest latency since they avoid network calls. They are useful for ephemeral computed values tied to a single instance, but they do not share state across instances, which means a cache miss on one instance may lead to repeated work elsewhere. Distributed caches like Redis or Memcached provide a shared store across instances. They scale and centralize cached state, but they introduce a small network hop and operational complexity. Imagine caching a computed product recommendation: in-process caching is fine for a single instance handling a burst of requests, but if you need consistent shared results and cross-instance reuse, a distributed cache is better. A common misconception is assuming distributed caches always improve latency; they can introduce hop latency but save much greater time by preventing expensive database queries. Key takeaway: match in-process caches to per-instance optimization and choose distributed caches when you need shared, scalable cache state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Application Cache

In-process vs Distributed Cache

Decide between lowest latency and shared state depending on your workload and scale.

In-process cache
Stored inside the application process: fastest access, limited to that instance, simple to implement.
Distributed cache
Centralized store like Redis shared across instances: scalable and consistent but introduces network hops and ops work.
Scenario
Cache session-affiliated computed values in-process for speed. Use Redis for shared counters, product caches, and results that benefit all instances.
Decision matrix
Latency
In-process wins on raw latency; distributed adds a small network delay.
Consistency
Distributed caches provide a single canonical cached state across instances.
Operational cost
Distributed caches require provisioning, monitoring, and failover planning.
Key takeaway
Use in-process for single-instance speed, distributed caches for shared, consistent cached data across a fleet.

screens.title: Database Cache
screens.narratorSegment: Databases maintain internal caches — buffer pools, index caches, and sometimes query caches — that keep frequently accessed pages and index blocks in memory. These caches are highly optimized for database operations and reduce disk input and output for repeated reads. However, they are the last line before hitting disk and do not replace higher-level caches when you need broader application-level offload. For example, a buffer pool speeds repeated row reads but won't reduce application-level query computation costs or avoid repeated complex joins. Some databases historically offered query caches that store full query results, but many have deprecated that feature because it creates concurrency and invalidation complexity. Use database caching to speed raw disk access and index lookups, but combine it with application-level or web server caches to reduce total load on the DB and to scale reads across many application instances. A common misconception is relying only on the DB cache to handle read spikes; it can be overwhelmed by concurrent queries and cannot absorb cross-application reuse as effectively as a distributed cache. Database Cache means db caches speed internal reads but are not a substitute for application or cdn caches for reducing overall origin load.. In practical terms, internal db caches and why they don’t replace higher-level caches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Database Cache

Database Caching

Buffer pools and index caches keep data pages in memory to speed reads, but they are not a replacement for higher-level caches.

Types
Buffer pool/page cache, index cache, and historically query caches in some systems.
Example
Repeated reads of hot rows are served from buffer pool pages rather than disk, reducing I/O latency.
Limitations & roles
Database caches help with disk-bound reads but do not provide application-level control or shared cross-instance caching semantics. Pair them with app and web caches to reduce load and scale reads efficiently.
Key takeaway
Treat DB caches as optimized storage for disk access; use higher-level caches to reduce query volume and expensive computation.

screens.title: Cache Hierarchy: Progressive Hit Path
screens.narratorSegment: A cache hierarchy arranges caches so requests first consult the fastest, closest caches and only fall back to slower or more expensive stores on a miss. A typical progressive path is: Browser cache → CDN edge → DNS resolution (to find edge) → Web server / reverse proxy → Application cache (Redis or in-process) → Database. Each layer reduces the chance the request must traverse to the next. The advantages are clear: the origin sees fewer requests, latency improves for repeat traffic, and cost is reduced. There are also costs: each added cache adds complexity for invalidation and increases the surface area for stale content. When designing the path, prioritize placing caches where they hit most often—static assets at the browser and CDN, expensive computed results at the application cache, and only use the database as the final source of truth. A useful design exercise is to map a single request such as fetching a frequently viewed product and mark where hits will likely occur. The core question to ask: which cache will deliver the biggest benefit for this asset while keeping consistency acceptable?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Cache Hierarchy

Progressive Hit Path

Arrange caches so a request checks the fastest layers first and only reaches slower layers on misses.

Typical sequence
Browser → CDN → Reverse proxy → App cache → Database. Each miss propagates to the next layer.
Example: product page
Image from browser/CDN, product metadata from CDN/app cache, stock and live pricing from database if necessary.
Common mistake
Treating each cache independently without coordinating invalidation and TTL policies across layers.
Design tips
  • Place the fastest caches nearest the user for static and repeatable hits.
  • Use shared caches for expensive compute results to avoid duplicate work across instances.
  • Coordinate TTLs and provide purge mechanisms when content updates are critical.
Key Takeaway
A layered cache strategy maximizes speed and resilience by catching requests at the closest fast caches before they reach slower systems.

screens.title: HTTP Caching Headers: ETag, Last-Modified, Cache-Control
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified is essential for browser caching behavior. In a simple simulated workflow, a server returns Cache-Control: max-age=300, Last-Modified with a timestamp, and an ETag token. On the first request the browser stores the resource and headers. Later, when the browser sends a conditional request with If-Modified-Since and If-None-Match, the server can respond with 304 Not Modified if nothing changed. This saves bandwidth because the full body is not resent. A practical exercise uses curl to simulate these steps: first request returns 200 with headers; the second sends conditional headers and gets 304; after the origin updates the resource, the conditional request returns 200 and the resource is updated. A common misconception is that 304 responses are slower than re-downloading; in practice, revalidation with 304 avoids the cost of transferring larger payloads and reduces server work. Try to explain how these headers together balance freshness and bandwidth savings: Cache-Control determines local TTL, ETag and Last-Modified enable safe revalidation, and 304 helps the client reuse its copy without fetching the full content. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: ETag and Last-Modified allow conditional requests; 304 Not Modified saves bandwidth and avoids full content transfer.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › HTTP Caching Headers

Simulated curl workflow

Observe how initial responses and conditional requests interact through headers and 304 responses.

First request — cache miss
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 1024
Content-Type: text/html
Last-Modified: Mon, 01 Jan 2024 10:00:00 GMT
ETag: "abc-123"
Cache-Control: max-age=300, public
Date: Mon, 01 Jan 2024 10:01:00 GMT

# ... body ...
Conditional request — revalidation
# If the resource is unchanged
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
Date: Mon, 01 Jan 2024 10:02:00 GMT
Cache-Control: max-age=300, public
Last-Modified: Mon, 01 Jan 2024 10:00:00 GMT
ETag: "abc-123"

# No body
After content change
If the origin updates the resource, the conditional request returns 200 with the new body and updated ETag/Last-Modified. The browser replaces its cached copy.
Why 304 matters
304 Not Modified avoids sending the full payload while ensuring the client still uses a valid copy. It balances freshness and bandwidth savings.
Try this mentally
Predict the headers you would receive when you make a second request before max-age expires, and after the origin updates the file.

screens.title: Trade-offs: Speed, Capacity, Consistency, Cost
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing where to cache is a multi-dimensional decision. Speed favors caches close to the user — browser and CDN — while capacity and shared state favor centralized caches and databases. Consistency often decreases as you move away from the origin: browser caches are least consistent from the server’s perspective, while the database is the canonical source of truth. Cost also varies: serving from a CDN may cost more than serving from an in-process cache but saves origin bandwidth and scale costs. When analyzing trade-offs, list the asset’s access pattern, acceptable staleness, and the cost of a cache miss. For example, an edge-cached static image can tolerate long TTLs and delivers huge latency wins and bandwidth savings. Conversely, a per-user session or live stock level is sensitive and better kept in a distributed cache with short TTLs or strong invalidation. A common misconception is optimizing for raw latency alone; the better design considers operational cost and correctness under failure. Build a small table for a specific resource: rank latency gain, hit rate expectation, cost, and consistency requirements. The outcome should be a pragmatic placement strategy aligned to the asset’s needs.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Trade-offs

Trade-off analysis

Rank assets against latency, capacity, consistency, and cost to decide where to cache.

Latency
Edge caches win for user-perceived latency.
Capacity
Central caches and CDNs provide much larger capacity than per-device browser caches.
Consistency & Cost
Choose the cache that meets freshness needs at an acceptable operational cost.
Practical checklist
  • Measure access patterns and hit rates before choosing TTLs and placement.
  • Estimate miss cost: database query time, network egress, compute spent on recomputing.
  • Prefer multi-layer caching to balance extremes — edge for latency, app caches for shared state, DB as fallback.
Key Takeaway
Make placement decisions with measurable metrics: access patterns, miss costs, and acceptable staleness guide the best tiering choices.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: We covered cache locality, the major cache tiers, and how to build a layered caching strategy. Remember that temporal locality is about recency and spatial locality is about related or neighboring data. Browser caches and CDNs serve static content near users for low latency; DNS caches speed up name lookups; web server caches absorb HTTP traffic; application caches offer flexible in-process or distributed options; databases cache disk pages internally but are not substitutes for higher-level caches. When designing a system, match cache placement to access patterns, acceptable staleness, and cost. Use multi-layer caching so the fastest, closest caches handle hot requests while slower caches and the database serve as fallbacks. A small checklist before you finish: identify the asset type, estimate likely hit rate, choose the tier that gives the biggest win for acceptable staleness, and ensure invalidation or versioning is planned.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll explore where to place caches in a distributed system, and why proximity to the consumer and the data source matters. You will learn the two core ideas of cache locality — temporal and spatial locality — and then see a practical map of typical cache tiers: browser, CDN, DNS, web server reverse proxy, application caches, and database caches. Each tier offers a different balance of speed, capacity, and consistency. For example, a browser cache gives you zero network latency for hits but limited capacity and control, whereas a distributed Redis cache gives shared state and control at the cost of network hops. We’ll also cover common mistakes, like overly aggressive cache headers or failing to purge CDN content. By the end you should be able to pick the right tier for static assets, A P I responses, and frequently accessed database records, and to explain why a multi-layered cache strategy often provides the best overall performance. Think about a request your app receives — which cache would you want it to hit first, and why?

By the end of this module you will be able to explain cache locality, recognize common cache tiers, evaluate trade-offs, and design a layered caching approach. First, you will learn the difference between temporal locality, where recently used data is likely to be used again, and spatial locality, where nearby data is likely to be accessed. Second, you will map caching tiers from browser and CDN down to application and database caches, noting speed and capacity differences. Third, you will weigh trade-offs such as latency, consistency, and cost when choosing where to cache. Finally, you will outline a multi-layer strategy that places caches to catch hot requests early while keeping slower, larger caches for broader coverage. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check when you’ve reached practical readiness. You’ll practice choosing a tier for example assets like images, A P I responses, and database records to reinforce these concepts.

This second objectives slide focuses on practicing the skills and the kinds of examples you should be confident with. You will practice picking cache tiers for specific asset types: static images should almost always be served by a CDN, small repeated A P I responses may be cached at the application or web server level, and frequently accessed DB rows benefit from a distributed cache. You will also practice reading HTTP headers and predicting cache behavior using conditional requests and ETag/Last-Modified interactions. Finally, the milestone check asks you to simulate a cache miss chain: predict which caches will be examined in order and why. Practicing these exercises translates conceptual knowledge into design decisions you'll explain in interviews and in real systems. A small set of mnemonics and a verification checklist are included so you can self-evaluate readiness before moving to hands-on activities.

Cache locality is the idea that some data is more likely to be accessed again soon, or that data near a recently accessed item will also be accessed. Temporal locality is simply recency: if a user just viewed a product page, they are likely to request related assets soon. Spatial locality is proximity: when you fetch a user record you often need nearby fields or related records like recent activity or addresses. These two principles shape caching behavior: temporal locality suggests keeping recently used items in fast caches; spatial locality suggests prefetching or caching surrounding data structures to reduce future misses. For example, an e-commerce product page load benefits from caching product metadata and adjacent stock levels because a user might open the reviews or similar products. A common misconception is treating all repeated access patterns as temporal locality — some workloads show locality only across related keys, not the identical key. That difference changes whether you design a time-based TTL or a prefetch rule for related keys. Key takeaway: match the cache strategy to observed access patterns — short TTLs for purely temporal hotspots, and grouped caches or prefetch for spatially correlated reads. To test your understanding, ask: does the workload ask for the same exact keys again, or for keys in the same cluster?

The browser cache is the cache closest to the user and can deliver assets with effectively zero network latency when a hit occurs. Browsers store static files — images, C S S, JavaScript, and sometimes entire H T M L responses — guided by HTTP headers like Cache-Control and Expires. This makes repeat visits much faster and reduces server bandwidth. However, capacity is limited by the browser and device, and developers have limited direct control: aggressive caching can cause stale content, while missing headers force unnecessary downloads. A concrete example: if a site serves a logo with Cache-Control: max-age=86400, the browser will reuse that logo for a day unless a conditional request is made. A common mistake is using long TTLs for dynamic content like user dashboards; that causes users to see stale personal data. Use browser caching for static, versioned assets and rely on cache-busting filenames or short TTLs with revalidation for assets that change. When choosing a cache strategy, think of the browser cache as the fastest but least controllable layer in the cache hierarchy. Browser Cache (Client-Side) means closest to user: fastest for hits but limited capacity and developer control; ideal for versioned static assets.. In practical terms, fast local storage for static assets with limited control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CDNs are geographically distributed proxy caches that bring static resources closer to users by storing copies on edge servers. When a user requests a file, the CDN routes the request to the nearest edge server and serves cached content if available, reducing latency and origin load. CDNs are ideal for large static assets, videos, and globally popular resources. They also sometimes cache dynamically generated content when configured with care. The trade-offs are clear: CDNs offer large capacity and global coverage, but they add an extra network hop and require an invalidation approach when origin content changes. For example, updating a site logo requires purging the cached object or versioning the filename, otherwise users may continue to see the old image. Security considerations include not caching sensitive personal data unless it is encrypted or properly segmented. A common mistake is trusting default CDN TTLs without aligning them to application semantics. Use CDNs for wide distribution of static assets and for reducing origin bandwidth; for frequently changing per-user data, prefer closer caches with better invalidation control. Content Delivery Network (CDN) means distributed edge cache for global performance; strong for static and broadly-accessed content, requires careful invalidation.. In practical terms, edge caching that brings content geographically closer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DNS caching is different from application caches because it caches name-to-IP mappings rather than resource content. DNS resolvers at the operating system, local resolver, and ISP level store records with a TTL so repeated lookups avoid full recursive resolution. This speeds the connection setup phase for users and lowers the cost of name resolution across the network. A TTL determines how long a record is considered valid. DNS caching is not a substitute for content caching, but it plays a crucial role in initial connection latency. A misconception is to treat short DNS TTLs as harmless — changing DNS frequently can lead to higher resolution load and potential propagation delays. Use appropriate TTLs: short for rapidly changing endpoints during migrations, longer for stable services. Remember, DNS impacts how quickly users reach your caches and origin, but it does not cache the payloads themselves. DNS Cache means caches domain-to-ip answers with ttls; reduces lookup latency but is not a content cache.. In practical terms, name resolution caching to speed connection setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A web server or reverse proxy cache sits at the edge of your server infrastructure and can absorb high volumes of requests before they reach application servers. Tools like Nginx can be configured to cache responses based on URL and headers and to set different TTLs per status code. This approach is effective for non-personalized content such as landing pages or A P I responses that are cacheable. Compared to an app cache, a web server cache is easier to deploy for full responses and can significantly reduce backend load. However, invalidation and personalization are more complex; personalized responses must bypass the cache or use vary headers. The provided Nginx config demonstrates basic caching: define the cache path and key, enable proxy_cache, and set proxy_cache_valid for TTL rules. A common pitfall is caching HTTP responses that include user-specific content without appropriate Vary headers or cache keys. Key takeaway: use reverse proxy caches for broad, non-personalizable responses and be explicit about keys and TTLs. Web Server Cache (Reverse Proxy) means caches application responses at the front door to reduce backend load; best for non-personalized content.. In practical terms, offload traffic at the entry point with nginx-style caching. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Application caching sits where your code runs and often determines the most strategic cache decisions in an architecture. There are two common forms: in-process caches and distributed caches. In-process caches live inside each application instance and offer the absolute lowest latency since they avoid network calls. They are useful for ephemeral computed values tied to a single instance, but they do not share state across instances, which means a cache miss on one instance may lead to repeated work elsewhere. Distributed caches like Redis or Memcached provide a shared store across instances. They scale and centralize cached state, but they introduce a small network hop and operational complexity. Imagine caching a computed product recommendation: in-process caching is fine for a single instance handling a burst of requests, but if you need consistent shared results and cross-instance reuse, a distributed cache is better. A common misconception is assuming distributed caches always improve latency; they can introduce hop latency but save much greater time by preventing expensive database queries. Key takeaway: match in-process caches to per-instance optimization and choose distributed caches when you need shared, scalable cache state.

Databases maintain internal caches — buffer pools, index caches, and sometimes query caches — that keep frequently accessed pages and index blocks in memory. These caches are highly optimized for database operations and reduce disk input and output for repeated reads. However, they are the last line before hitting disk and do not replace higher-level caches when you need broader application-level offload. For example, a buffer pool speeds repeated row reads but won't reduce application-level query computation costs or avoid repeated complex joins. Some databases historically offered query caches that store full query results, but many have deprecated that feature because it creates concurrency and invalidation complexity. Use database caching to speed raw disk access and index lookups, but combine it with application-level or web server caches to reduce total load on the DB and to scale reads across many application instances. A common misconception is relying only on the DB cache to handle read spikes; it can be overwhelmed by concurrent queries and cannot absorb cross-application reuse as effectively as a distributed cache. Database Cache means db caches speed internal reads but are not a substitute for application or cdn caches for reducing overall origin load.. In practical terms, internal db caches and why they don’t replace higher-level caches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A cache hierarchy arranges caches so requests first consult the fastest, closest caches and only fall back to slower or more expensive stores on a miss. A typical progressive path is: Browser cache → CDN edge → DNS resolution (to find edge) → Web server / reverse proxy → Application cache (Redis or in-process) → Database. Each layer reduces the chance the request must traverse to the next. The advantages are clear: the origin sees fewer requests, latency improves for repeat traffic, and cost is reduced. There are also costs: each added cache adds complexity for invalidation and increases the surface area for stale content. When designing the path, prioritize placing caches where they hit most often—static assets at the browser and CDN, expensive computed results at the application cache, and only use the database as the final source of truth. A useful design exercise is to map a single request such as fetching a frequently viewed product and mark where hits will likely occur. The core question to ask: which cache will deliver the biggest benefit for this asset while keeping consistency acceptable?

Understanding Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified is essential for browser caching behavior. In a simple simulated workflow, a server returns Cache-Control: max-age=300, Last-Modified with a timestamp, and an ETag token. On the first request the browser stores the resource and headers. Later, when the browser sends a conditional request with If-Modified-Since and If-None-Match, the server can respond with 304 Not Modified if nothing changed. This saves bandwidth because the full body is not resent. A practical exercise uses curl to simulate these steps: first request returns 200 with headers; the second sends conditional headers and gets 304; after the origin updates the resource, the conditional request returns 200 and the resource is updated. A common misconception is that 304 responses are slower than re-downloading; in practice, revalidation with 304 avoids the cost of transferring larger payloads and reduces server work. Try to explain how these headers together balance freshness and bandwidth savings: Cache-Control determines local TTL, ETag and Last-Modified enable safe revalidation, and 304 helps the client reuse its copy without fetching the full content. Choosing where to cache is a multi-dimensional decision. Speed favors caches close to the user — browser and CDN — while capacity and shared state favor centralized caches and databases. Consistency often decreases as you move away from the origin: browser caches are least consistent from the server’s perspective, while the database is the canonical source of truth. Cost also varies: serving from a CDN may cost more than serving from an in-process cache but saves origin bandwidth and scale costs. When analyzing trade-offs, list the asset’s access pattern, acceptable staleness, and the cost of a cache miss. For example, an edge-cached static image can tolerate long TTLs and delivers huge latency wins and bandwidth savings. Conversely, a per-user session or live stock level is sensitive and better kept in a distributed cache with short TTLs or strong invalidation. A common misconception is optimizing for raw latency alone; the better design considers operational cost and correctness under failure. Build a small table for a specific resource: rank latency gain, hit rate expectation, cost, and consistency requirements. The outcome should be a pragmatic placement strategy aligned to the asset’s needs.

We covered cache locality, the major cache tiers, and how to build a layered caching strategy. Remember that temporal locality is about recency and spatial locality is about related or neighboring data. Browser caches and CDNs serve static content near users for low latency; DNS caches speed up name lookups; web server caches absorb HTTP traffic; application caches offer flexible in-process or distributed options; databases cache disk pages internally but are not substitutes for higher-level caches. When designing a system, match cache placement to access patterns, acceptable staleness, and cost. Use multi-layer caching so the fastest, closest caches handle hot requests while slower caches and the database serve as fallbacks. A small checklist before you finish: identify the asset type, estimate likely hit rate, choose the tier that gives the biggest win for acceptable staleness, and ensure invalidation or versioning is planned.

These additional reminders help you implement caching safely. Web server reverse proxies absorb traffic for non-personalized responses. Application caches — in-process or distributed — should be chosen based on whether you need shared state across instances. Database caches speed internal IO but do not substitute for application caches. Always plan invalidation: TTLs, purges, or versioned asset names are necessary to avoid stale content. When in doubt, measure: hit rates, miss cost, and the user impact of staleness will guide your final decisions. Use the progressive cache path as a design template, and practice mapping sample requests through it until you can explain why a chosen tier is the best fit.
